title: Prepared for anything, above ground or below: A glimpse at emergency readiness and first response in potash operations
summary: A behind‑the‑scenes look at emergency readiness and first response at Nutrien’s potash operations, where safety is a constant mindset above and below ground.
body_text: Before potash ever reaches trains, ships and farmers’ fields, the people who mine and produce it must be safe. At Nutrien, safety isn’t a checklist, it’s a permanent mindset that applies everywhere, every day, and doesn’t switch off at the end of a shift. “I cut the grass with earplugs and boots on,” says Kurt Wallace, ERT Coordinator at our Allan Potash site. “It’s instilled, so I take safety home with me.” That always‑on mindset is backed by real emergency readiness. While some potash operations are closer to municipal emergency services than others, every site has trained teams ready to respond immediately when minutes matter. Kurt Wallace, ERT Coordinator, Allan ERTs (Emergency Response Teams) are based above ground, while Mine Rescue Teams are below ground. They are equipped to act as first responders in fires, medical emergencies, rescues and other serious incidents. They coordinate closely with external emergency services when needed. Kurt and other ERT coordinators lead emergency response and oversee regular site training. Skills are practiced and refined through monthly training sessions that cover a wide range of realistic scenarios, from medical incidents and rescues to fire response and emergency stabilization. Nutrien emergency vehicle, Allan In some cases, teams may meet an ambulance halfway on the highway. In others, they can safely transport someone with a less serious injury directly to hospital. More often, they provide critical early care, such as administering first aid, oxygen, monitoring vital signs and stabilizing patients until additional support arrives. “It’s the kind of readiness most people never see, but it’s what allows operations to keep moving safely, day after day, in a way people can depend on,” says Leslie Frehlich, GM, Allan Potash site. “We operate in environments where conditions can change quickly. When something goes wrong, preparation and training make all the difference, which is why we invest so heavily in our emergency response teams and treat safety as a mindset, not a moment.” 2025 Mining Week, Emergency Response Competition ERT capabilities are most visible during annual mine rescue competitions, where teams demonstrate skills comparable to firefighters. But the same training carries into everyday life. Many ERT members also serve as volunteer firefighters in their communities, or step in as calm, capable good Samaritans when emergencies happen off the job. For the most part, preparedness happens quietly, behind the scenes. Did you know? All potash sites are equipped with dedicated emergency vehicles and firefighting equipment Emergency response coverage is available 24/7 at every site Nearby potash sites can provide mutual aid in serious emergency situations ERTs are trained to respond to fires, serious incidents, medical emergencies, rescues, hazardous materials and more Monthly training and mock scenarios keep skills sharp While safety is everyone’s responsibility, having on‑site emergency teams ready to respond adds a critical layer of protection. ERTs don’t just model safe choices, they help set the standard through preparation, judgment and teamwork that makes reliable, responsible operations possible. “To me, a culture of safety is a culture of care,” says Kurt. “You need to care about your fellow workers and your fellow people.”

title: Deploy AI Customer Support in 2 Weeks, Not 6 Months
summary: Duckie deploys in 2 weeks because self-building AI generates runbooks from your ticket history, no services team, no 6-month implementation, no AI engineers required.
body_text: Duckie deploys in 2 weeks because self-building AI generates runbooks from your ticket history, no services team, no 6-month implementation, no AI engineers required. The 2-week deployment claim is the one Duckie customers cite most often when talking to other support leaders, and the one that gets the most skepticism before they see it. Six months is the industry default for enterprise AI support. Decagon, Sierra, and full Zendesk AI implementations with professional services all run in that range. The question is not whether the 6-month number is real. It is why Duckie does not need it. The answer is self-building AI. The mechanism that compresses deployment from a quarter-long engineering project to a two-week support-team project is not a simpler product or fewer features. It is a fundamentally different architecture for how the AI gets ready to work. Why competitors take 6 months The 6-month timeline for enterprise AI support is a services model, not a technology constraint. Platforms like Decagon and Sierra do not come with pre-built runbooks, the policy documents that tell the AI what to do when a refund request lands, when to escalate, what thresholds apply, and which API calls to make. Writing those runbooks, testing them against real ticket scenarios, building integrations with your specific payment system and account database, handling edge cases and failure modes, and validating behavior before going live is real work. It takes AI engineers, integration developers, and quality reviewers. The contract structure reflects this: the deployment fee is not for software licenses. It is for the professional services team that does the implementation work. When that team finishes, the system is live. Until they finish, it is not. This model works. It also means six months pass before you see the first ticket close. The bottleneck was always implementation, not AI capability The core claim of self-building AI is that the implementation work does not need to be done by humans. An AI agent trained on your ticket history can read 10,000 past tickets, identify the common patterns, and generate draft runbooks that reflect what your support team has been doing manually. It surfaces what thresholds your agents have been implicitly using, which ticket types always escalate, and which responses have historically resolved the request. Those drafts are not perfect. Your support team reviews them, edits for accuracy, sets explicit thresholds, and catches anything the AI got wrong. But the starting point is a working draft for every major ticket category, not a blank document that a services team builds from scratch over weeks. This is the difference between six months and two weeks. The AI does the drafting. The support team does the editing. No AI engineering team is in the loop. What a 2-week Duckie deployment actually looks like The two-week timeline is not a marketing claim with a footnote. Here is the actual sequence: Day 1–2: Connect your helpdesk (Zendesk, Intercom, Freshdesk, HubSpot, Pylon, or Plain) and knowledge sources (Confluence, Notion, Google Drive, or Guru). The integration is pre-built, no custom development. Duckie ingests historical tickets and begins generating runbook drafts. Day 2–5: Runbook drafts are ready for review. Your support team reads through each one in plain language, no code, no configuration UI, just policy statements. Edits happen in real time. Escalation thresholds get set explicitly. Day 5–7: Shadow mode activates. Duckie processes incoming tickets and generates decisions without acting on them. Your team reviews the shadow decisions daily. Any runbook gaps or edge cases surface here. Day 7–14: Shadow mode validates. The team approves go-live for the categories where shadow decisions consistently matched what a human agent would have done. Day 14: Go live. Auto-resolution activates. Tickets in covered categories close without human intervention. The timeline can compress. For teams with clean historical tickets and well-organized knowledge bases, shadow mode validates faster. It can also extend - by a week, not a quarter - if the ticket history is sparse or the backend integrations are highly custom. The proof: Vanquish and Grid Vanquish, a high-volume trading fintech, deployed Duckie in under one week. Their ticket history was well-organized, their helpdesk was Intercom, and their key action, balance inquiries and transaction verifications, was deterministic enough to validate in shadow mode quickly. They were live in five days. Resolution rate: 94%. Grid, a consumer fintech with 15,000 monthly support tickets, deployed in two weeks. Their ticket mix was more varied - refunds, account verifications, KYC-related questions - and shadow mode ran for a full week before go-live. Resolution rate: 91%. Both deployments happened without an AI engineering team. The support team at each company did the runbook review. An integration with Stripe and the existing helpdesk was the technical surface area. That is representative of most deployments on standard stacks. What you need to have The two-week timeline has preconditions. The faster deployments happen when these are already in place: A working helpdesk on one of the supported platforms: Zendesk, Intercom, Freshdesk, HubSpot, Pylon, or Plain. A knowledge base that Duckie can use to draft runbooks: Confluence, Notion, Google Drive, or Guru. Unstructured or siloed documentation slows down runbook generation. Ticket history : at least a few hundred tickets across the major categories. The richer the history, the better the initial runbook drafts. Backend system credentials if action capabilities (refunds, account updates) are in scope: Stripe API keys for payment actions, access to the relevant account database for profile updates. If the knowledge base is scattered or ticket history is thin, the runbook drafts require more editing. That adds time. The deployment still does not take six months, but the two-week estimate becomes three. What "no AI team required" actually means The phrase "no AI engineers required" can mean a lot of different things depending on what the product actually asks you to do. For Duckie, it means: Runbooks are edited in plain language. No prompt engineering, no JSON configuration, no model fine-tuning. Integrations are pre-built. Connecting Stripe, Zendesk, or Confluence does not require a developer. Shadow mode requires no instrumentation. It runs automatically when you turn it on. Going live is a toggle. No deployment pipeline, no engineering sign-off. The support team leads the deployment. Your Head of Support makes the go-live call. An engineer may need to be involved if the backend system requires a custom API key or a non-standard authentication setup, but that is an hour-long task, not a sprint. This matters because support teams move differently from engineering teams. A support team can review a runbook draft, push back on an escalation threshold, and approve a category for auto-resolution in a two-week sprint. A six-month professional services engagement is not something a support team controls, it is something that happens to them. Self-building AI puts the deployment timeline in the hands of the people who know the ticket categories best. The tradeoff Two-week deployment is real, with the caveats described above. What it is not is maintenance-free. New ticket categories, new product features, and new edge cases will require runbook updates. The difference from the services model is that those updates happen on a support-team timescale, a runbook edit reviewed and approved in a day, not a change request that queues behind a services contract. The ongoing maintenance model is the same as the deployment model: the AI proposes, the support team approves. The team that deployed in two weeks is the same team that keeps it running. See it in action Integrations Helpdesks, CRMs, and backend systems Duckie plugs into. Duckie: AI support agents See how Duckie resolves tickets end-to-end. Frequently asked questions Two weeks for most companies on standard stacks (Zendesk or Intercom plus a knowledge base). Week one covers integration and AI-generated runbook drafts. Week two covers support team review, shadow mode, and go-live. Enterprise platforms like Decagon and Sierra typically run six months or more due to professional services implementation. The 6-month timeline reflects services-model implementation: a team of AI engineers writes runbooks, builds integrations, handles failure modes, and tests the system before go-live. That work is real, it just is not necessary when self-building AI generates runbooks automatically from your ticket history. No. Duckie generates its own runbook drafts from historical tickets. Your support team reviews and edits them in plain language. The integrations are pre-built for common helpdesks and payment systems. The entire deployment is run by the support team, no AI engineers, no services contract. A working helpdesk (Zendesk, Intercom, Freshdesk, HubSpot, Pylon, or Plain) and a knowledge base (Confluence, Notion, Google Drive, or Guru). The AI uses ticket history to generate runbooks, the more structured your historical tickets, the faster the runbook generation. Backend system credentials (Stripe, account database) are needed for action capabilities. Vanquish, a high-volume trading fintech, deployed Duckie in under one week. Grid, a consumer fintech with 15,000 monthly tickets, was live in two weeks. Both are on standard helpdesk and Stripe stacks, no custom implementation required.

Cosmic AI Agents vs. Contentful Skills: Two Very Different Visions of AI in the CMS
summary: Contentful Skills and Cosmic AI Agents both bring AI into the CMS, but the approaches are completely different. Here's what each one actually does and which fits your team.
body_text: On May 20, 2026, Contentful announced Contentful Skills: a free, open-source package that teaches your AI coding agent how to build on Contentful. It works with Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and a dozen other AI coding tools. It is genuinely well-built and solves a real problem for Contentful developers. We're not going to dismiss it. We're going to explain why it and Cosmic AI Agents are solving fundamentally different problems, and why that difference matters for how you think about AI in your content stack. What Contentful Skills Actually Does Contentful Skills ships as four installable skill packages: contentful-guide : Core concepts and routing, helps the AI coding agent decide which skill to use. contentful-nextjs : SDK setup, content fetching, and Draft Mode previews for Next.js App Router and Pages Router. contentful-migration : Writes and runs content model migration scripts. contentful-personalization : Four interactive workflows covering onboarding, live debugging, health checks, and ongoing development. The personalization skill is the flagship. It can open a real Chrome session, inspect a running page, and cross-reference it with your codebase to debug why a variant isn't rendering. That's impressive tooling. The frame Contentful uses is accurate: "Developers don't live in documentation anymore. They live in their AI coding agent." So Contentful built a way to live there too. What Contentful Skills does, plainly stated: it makes developers faster at building on Contentful. It is a coding assistant that understands Contentful's content model, SDK, and personalization layer. When you ask your coding agent a question about Contentful, it now has context-aware, codebase-aware answers instead of generic ones. That is the product. It is a copilot for developers working in Contentful. What Cosmic AI Agents Actually Do Cosmic AI Agents are not coding assistants. They are autonomous actors that operate inside your organization's workflows, whether or not a developer is present. Here's the concrete breakdown by agent type: Team Agents Team Agents live inside Slack, WhatsApp, and Telegram. They have persistent memory across conversations, respond to messages from real team members, and take action based on what they're asked. A Team Agent can receive a Slack message like "Write a blog post about our Q2 product update and publish it to the CMS" and do exactly that, without anyone opening a code editor or a CMS dashboard. They support scheduled heartbeat check-ins, meaning they can proactively surface information on a schedule, not just when asked. Content Agents Content Agents create, update, and manage CMS content autonomously. They run on a schedule or are triggered by webhooks. They can generate articles, update existing content objects in bulk, run content migrations, and publish or unpublish content based on rules. No developer needs to be in the loop. Code Agents Code Agents connect directly to GitHub repositories. They can build features, fix bugs, create pull requests, and deploy to production or preview environments, all on isolated git branches. When a Code Agent finishes its work, it opens a PR for human review. The human reviews the code; the agent did the work. Computer Use Agents Computer Use Agents automate browser tasks using visual AI. They can record demo videos, cross-post media between platforms, extract data from websites, and execute any workflow that requires navigating a browser, all without human intervention. Workflows All four agent types can be chained together using Workflows. A Workflow might look like: a Content Agent writes a blog post, a Code Agent deploys the page, and a Team Agent posts a summary to Slack, all triggered by a single webhook when a product update lands in your CMS. Workflows run on schedules or fire on events. And all of this integrates with Cosmic's MCP Server and Agent Skills for Cursor, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot, so developers working in AI coding environments have Cosmic context too, when they need it. The Philosophical Difference: Copilot vs. Autonomous Operator This is where the two products diverge at the root level. Contentful Skills makes a developer more effective. The developer is still the actor. They type a prompt into their coding agent, the skill provides better guidance, and the developer writes better code faster. The human is in the loop at every step. This is the copilot model, and it's a good one. Cosmic AI Agents remove the developer from the loop entirely for tasks that don't require them. A marketing manager can message an agent in Slack and get a published blog post. A content ops team can schedule an agent to monitor and update product descriptions every night. A Code Agent can respond to a bug report, fix it, open a PR, and notify the team, all while everyone sleeps. The question isn't which approach is better in the abstract. The question is: what problem are you trying to solve? If your problem is that Contentful is hard to set up and your developers waste time in documentation: Contentful Skills is a well-targeted solution. If your problem is that content creation, publishing, code deployment, and distribution require too many humans doing too much manual work: you need autonomous agents. Side-by-Side Comparison Contentful Skills Cosmic AI Agents Category AI coding assistant Autonomous AI operators Who uses it Developers Developers, marketers, content teams, anyone Where it lives Inside your AI coding tool (Cursor, Copilot, Claude Code) Slack, WhatsApp, Telegram, scheduled jobs, webhooks Primary action Answers questions, guides code Creates content, commits code, deploys, distributes Human in the loop Always Optional Content creation No Yes, autonomously Code execution Guided (human writes the code) Direct (agent commits and deploys) Scheduling No Yes, schedules and webhook triggers CMS integration Deep (Contentful-specific) Native (Cosmic is the CMS) Multi-channel messaging No Yes, Slack + WhatsApp + Telegram Workflows No Yes, multi-agent chains MCP Server Yes Yes Open source Yes (Skills package) Agent Skills for coding tools Real Capabilities, Not Marketing Claims Let's be concrete about what Cosmic AI Agents can do right now: A content team lead messages their Slack agent: "We need a blog post comparing headless CMS options for Next.js teams, targeting 'best headless CMS Next.js' as the primary keyword. Publish it as a draft and send me a summary." The Team Agent researches the topic using web browsing, writes the article with proper SEO structure, creates a featured image, saves it as a draft in Cosmic, and posts a summary back to Slack, including a link to review. No developer. No dashboard login. One message. An engineering team sets up a weekly Code Agent: Every Monday at 9am, the agent checks for open GitHub issues tagged , writes fixes on isolated branches, opens PRs with descriptions, and posts the PR links to the #engineering Slack channel for review. A marketing team runs a multi-agent Workflow: When a new product feature ships (webhook trigger), a Content Agent drafts the announcement blog post, a Team Agent posts a teaser to the company's Slack, and a Computer Use Agent records a short demo video for the social team. All automated, all logged. This is what "autonomous" means in practice: workflows that run without someone manually initiating each step. On the MCP Server and Agent Skills Cosmic does offer an MCP Server and Agent Skills for Cursor, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot, so developers working in AI coding environments get Cosmic context when they need it. This is the overlap with Contentful Skills. But it's a small part of the Cosmic AI story, not the center of it. The center is agents that operate on your behalf, not tools that assist you while you operate. Pricing, Access, and Getting Started Contentful Skills is free and open-source. Install it and your coding agent gets Contentful context. That's a genuinely good deal for Contentful developers. You can build your first autonomous agent workflow today without spending anything. The Bottom Line Contentful Skills is a thoughtful developer tool. It solves a real problem for teams already on Contentful who want AI coding agents to understand their platform better. If you're in that boat, it's worth installing. Cosmic AI Agents are a different category of product. They don't just help you build faster. They do the work: writing content, deploying code, distributing across channels, and reporting back, all without requiring a human to trigger each step. One product accelerates a developer. The other replaces the workflow. If you're evaluating where AI fits in your content and development stack in 2026, that distinction is worth understanding before you commit to a platform. That’s the power of fresh juice. Thinking about investing in a commercial juicer? Here’s what you need to know. The benefits of a centrifugal juice extractor Customer experience: A centrifugal commercial juice extractor is designed for single-batch juicing. It’s made right there in the shop, so customers can see firsthand that they’re getting the freshest possible product. Cold-pressed juice, on the other hand, is typically manufactured offsite and bottled. Pulp content: Pulp is a key element of juice flavor and appearance. More pulp means more flavor, but also creates a thicker consistency that’s not for everyone. However, low pulp levels mean juice separates more rapidly when displayed on ice, which isn’t great for visual appeal. otto™ the Juice Extractor is designed to hit the sweet spot: 3-3.5% pulp for ideal flavor, color and consistency. Speed and ease of use: For freshly made juice, profits depend on how fast the operator can make each serving. otto™ is made to streamline each step of the process: Large-diameter chute to reduce prep time Ergonomic food pusher for efficient loading Special spout and oversized drip tray keep counter clean Stainless steel components and large pulp bin that are easily removed for rapid cleaning Yield: Yield — the amount of juice obtained from fresh produce — is key for busy juice shops. If there’s a lot of juice left in the pulp, you’re losing money. otto™’s blades and strainer basket are designed to extract the maximum amount of juice from a wide variety of fruits and vegetables. To maximize yield, one rule of thumb is to add the most fibrous produce first, such as kale, spinach, celery, and ginger. Afterward, add juicier ingredients, like apples or cucumbers. Durability: If you read reviews of cheap commercial juice extractors, a common complaint is that they break easily or get stuck. The health benefits of a centrifugal juicer vs. cold-pressed juicer Much has been said about the health benefits of cold-pressed juice vs. juice made with a centrifugal juicer. The claim: Cold-pressed juices are better for you, because the slight amount of heat generated by the spinning blades of a centrifugal juicer can reduce the bioactive compounds present in fresh produce. Because of this, cold-pressed juices are typically sold at premium prices. However, research has shown that there is no real difference in the health benefits of cold-pressed juice vs. centrifugal juice. If you want the specifics, here’s what the researchers said : “We observed no significant differences between cold-pressed and normal centrifugal juices in terms of the contents of bioactive compounds (ascorbic acid, total phenolic, and total carotenoid) and antioxidant capacity (ferric ion reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) and 1,1-diphenyl-2-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical scavenging activity).” What about citrus juicing? There’s just no substitute for the bright, lively taste of freshly squeezed orange juice. Why does it taste so much better? Packaged orange juice is pasteurized to kill harmful bacteria, which changes its flavor. So orange juice bottlers use “flavor packs” to make their product taste better: chemical compounds derived from orange oil and orange peels. That’s why freshly squeezed orange juice — whether served on its own, in a cocktail, or in a smoothie — is such a treat for customers. All you need is the FreshMark™ Electric Citrus Juicer . body_text: Scaling fan conventions from a cozy 2,000-person gathering into a 100,000-attendee mega-event is both thrilling and daunting. On one hand, more fans mean bigger guest stars, expansive programming, and increased revenue opportunities. On the other, rapid growth can strain logistics and risk losing the intimate community vibe that made the convention special. The good news: many fan events have successfully made this leap by planning carefully and prioritizing fan experience. It is possible to grow convention attendance dramatically without sacrificing the magic – but it requires veteran insight and strategic scaling at every step. Fan conventions have exploded into the mainstream in recent years, with attendance surging at major events around the world . For example, Dragon Con in Atlanta started with just 1,200 attendees at an Atlanta hotel in the late ’80s and now draws over 65,000 fans across five downtown hotels each year – bringing an $80 million boost to the local economy. New York Comic Con has surpassed 200,000 attendees in 2023, even overtaking San Diego Comic-Con’s ~150,000 as the largest comic convention in North America . These events grew exponentially over decades, learning hard lessons along the way. In this guide, we’ll explore how to replicate that success in 2026 and beyond , scaling your fan convention without losing operational sanity or the close-knit feel that attendees cherish. Expect practical strategies earned through experience: how to expand programming and guest lineups as crowds grow; when to upgrade venues (or add new ones) to handle the masses; ways to recruit and organize a volunteer army; technology tools to streamline everything from ticketing to crowd communication; and tactics to keep fan communities engaged and happy even as the event balloons in size. We’ll spotlight real examples of conventions that navigated growth expertly – and cautionary tales of those that stumbled. Whether you’re growing a fan convention for comics, anime, gaming, sci-fi, or all of the above, these insights will help you scale up while keeping the magic alive . Laying the Groundwork to Grow Convention Attendance Setting a Scalable Vision and Pace Growing a fan convention successfully starts with a clear vision and realistic pacing. Organizers should decide early on why they want to scale up. Are you aiming to become a multi-genre pop culture expo, or to remain focused on a niche fandom while welcoming more people? Having a north-star vision helps guide which opportunities to pursue and which to decline as you expand. Convention veterans recommend creating a multi-year growth roadmap – for example, targeting a 15–20% attendance increase per year rather than a sudden jump from 2,000 to 10,000 in one go. Gradual growth allows your team to learn and adjust in stages, preventing attendee experience from collapsing under too-steep a climb. As one con organizer put it, “scale responsibly – you want each year’s attendees to leave excited for more, not vowing never to return.” Scaling Your Convention Vision Responsibly — Gradual growth ensures your infrastructure and team can keep pace with rising attendance without breaking the fan experience. It’s also wise to study how similar events grew. Look at attendance trends for comparable cons in your region or genre. If local anime and comic conventions have been growing 10% annually, that’s a reasonable benchmark for your event’s natural growth without overreach. Some conventions even cap attendance in certain years to protect the fan experience, a strategy used by events like Anime NYC and others to avoid overcrowding when a venue hasn’t caught up . The goal is to build momentum year over year – but not at the expense of long lines, safety hazards, or a loss of charm. By pacing growth, you can scale up excitement and infrastructure in tandem. Community-Building and Word-of-Mouth Marketing In the early stages, nothing beats fan-driven marketing to grow convention attendance. Your existing attendees are your best ambassadors. Tapping into this through referral incentives and community engagement can boost numbers significantly without huge ad spends. For instance, launching a fan convention referral program can turn passionate attendees into a street team for your event. Many cons have seen attendance jump 15–25% by empowering fans to spread the word . Simple tactics like giving a discount or exclusive pin for every friend referred can multiply your reach. (One 2022 fan expo generated over $100,000 in extra ticket sales by rewarding superfans who recruited others.) Organizers can leverage social media challenges, con-specific hashtags, and “bring a friend” campaigns to amplify the FOMO and excitement. Ready to Sell Tickets? Create professional event pages with built-in payment processing, marketing tools, and real-time analytics. Create Your Event Event Ticketing Software Beyond referrals, invest in year-round community building so that your convention’s fanbase grows in tandem with the event. This might mean hosting an official Discord or Facebook group, running mini meetups or online panels between annual events, and featuring fan art or cosplay spotlights on your blog. Engaging media and influencers can help as well – e.g. inviting popular cosplayers or content creators to be guests, which brings their followers to your con. Just be sure any promotional push is matched by operational readiness. Successful organizers align their marketing with capacity; they’ll open up more badge batches only when additional venue space or staff are secured. The worst outcome is to over-hype and oversell beyond what your con can handle (as the ill-fated TanaCon learned when thousands showed up to a venue built for a few hundred). By growing your audience organically and scaling operations in lockstep, you set a strong foundation for sustainable expansion. Expanding Programming and Guest Lineups Diversifying Content Tracks as You Scale One of the biggest appeals of a larger convention is the sheer variety of programming on offer. To grow from a handful of panels to a packed schedule spanning multiple stages, start by diversifying your content tracks . For example, a small 2,000-person anime con might have had one main events room and two panel rooms; a 50,000-person version could support dedicated tracks for anime, manga, cosplay, gaming, K-pop, and more, each running simultaneously. Look at what adjacent fandom interests your attendees have and gradually introduce new tracks to broaden the event’s scope. Many conventions cross-pollinate genres as they grow – a comic con might add an esports gaming arena, an anime con might introduce an artist alley and science-fiction panels. These additions attract new attendee segments and justify a higher ticket price, while keeping core fans entertained rather than stuck in one overcrowded room. Managing an expanded programme requires tools and strategy. Scheduling becomes an art form at scale – you’ll be coordinating dozens (even hundreds) of panels, screenings, workshops, and performances across multiple days. It helps to bring on a dedicated programming team or use scheduling software to organise time slots and avoid major content overlaps that frustrate fans. Some large cons even repeat especially popular panels or run encore screenings later in the weekend so more people can experience them. As attendance grows, consider tiered access or reservations for high-demand content. For instance, San Diego Comic-Con’s famous Hall H film studio panels require overnight wristbands to manage the massive lines, and some big conventions use online lotteries or pre-registration for panels to fairly allocate limited seats. The larger your event, the more you need structured systems like this to keep programming accessible and avoid endless queues. Real-world case studies show the value of proactive programming expansion. New York Comic Con, upon hitting around 100,000 attendees, didn’t just add more panels – it spread them across the city. By 2018, NYCC was hosting over 420 panel sessions across seven venues (the Javits Center plus six nearby sites like Madison Square Garden). This multi-venue approach allowed a wider variety of content (comics, TV, anime, gaming, etc.) without overcrowding one building. It also meant creating a robust shuttle and scheduling system to coordinate sessions and attendee movement between locations. The takeaway: more attendees = more interests to satisfy . Expanding your content offerings in a thoughtful, organised way lets a 100,000-person con feel like several great smaller cons under one roof , where each fan can find their niche. Navigating The Multi-Venue Campus Model — Spreading programming across several specialized locations prevents overcrowding while maintaining a vibrant, city-wide festival atmosphere. Managing Bigger Guest Rosters (Without the Drama) As conventions scale up, so do their guest lineups – and the complexity of managing them. A small con might feature a few local artists or voice actors who mix freely with fans. A mega-con will host A-list celebrity actors, directors, pro gamers, bestselling authors, and beyond. To attract marquee names that draw crowds, be prepared to negotiate appearance fees and logistics months in advance . Top-tier Hollywood talent may charge anywhere from $25,000 to $250,000+ for a convention appearance, plus travel, lodging, and per-diems. It’s critical to budget for these fees (and perhaps secure sponsors to underwrite them) before you promise a huge guest. Knowing the tiers – e.g. TV stars vs. film stars vs. internet influencers – will help set realistic expectations for who you can afford at each growth stage. Some big conventions use a mix: a few headline celebrities to drive buzz, supported by many mid-tier guests (comic artists, voice actors, authors, niche icons) that collectively appeal to diverse fandoms. Large guest rosters also mean you’ll need a professional guest relations team . Assign experienced handlers or liaisons to each VIP guest to manage their schedules, assist with queues, and enforce their contract terms (like no off-schedule autographs, or limits on personal photo-taking). Create a detailed green room and panel schedule for all guests – at 2,000 attendees you could get by with a casual approach, but at 50,000+, any missed communication can lead to a panel with no panelists or a frustrated star who didn’t realize fans would mob them on the show floor. Treat your guests well with clear itineraries, private backstage areas, and smooth transportation; in return, they’ll be more likely to return and give fans a great experience. Sell Tickets Online Get Started Free Another key is structuring autograph and photo op sessions as you scale. In small events these can be informal, but in huge cons they become major undertakings. Consider using separate ticketed autograph sessions for the most famous guests to control the demand (fans either purchase a limited autograph ticket or enter a raffle). This not only manages lines but can offset high appearance fees. Ensure you have line caps and overflow plans – nothing enrages attendees like waiting three hours only to be turned away. Use line staff or virtual queue systems to give real-time updates (“the Mark Hamill signing is now full”) so people can enjoy other activities instead of standing in a hopeless queue. By taking a page from veterans – such as understanding how major cons negotiate celebrity contracts and schedule signings – you can avoid common pitfalls. The larger your convention grows, the more your guest operations should run like a well-oiled machine, with clear rules, plenty of staff, and contingency plans for everything (including inevitable last-minute guest cancellations). Pull it off and your attendees will rave about meeting their heroes without chaos – a hallmark of a big convention that hasn’t lost its fan-first charm. Managing High-Profile Celebrity Guest Logistics — Professional handlers and structured backstage workflows ensure a smooth, stress-free experience for both stars and their fans. Upgrading Venues, Logistics, and Crowd Flow Finding the Right Venue (or Venues ) for Each Stage Your venue is arguably the single biggest factor in how large your convention can grow. Many fan events originate in modest venues – perhaps a university hall or hotel ballroom that comfortably holds a couple thousand people. As attendance pushes past that threshold, you’ll face a major decision: expand or move . Some conventions take an interim step of adding an extra day (spreading 5,000 attendees over three days instead of two, for example) or using overflow space at adjacent facilities. But eventually, to hit 10,000, 20,000, or 100,000 attendees, you need significantly more square footage and likely a purpose-built convention center. When upgrading venue, think long term. If you’ve outgrown a 30,000 sq ft venue, don’t jump to just a 50,000 sq ft one if projections show you’ll hit capacity again in two years. It might be better to move into a major convention center or exhibition hall that offers room to grow over 5–10 years. Also consider geography – will relocating to a bigger city bring in more fans and guests, or alienate your original community? Some cons solve this by spreading across multiple venues in the same city instead of one giant hall. For example, as mentioned, New York Comic Con utilizes the main Javits Convention Center plus satellite theaters and event halls for special programming. Dragon Con in Atlanta takes over five large hotels within a few blocks, effectively creating a walkable “campus” of different themed venues (sci-fi in one hotel, gaming in another, etc.). This multi-venue strategy can preserve a close-knit feel by breaking the mega-event into distinct zones, though it requires tight coordination and clear attendee guidance. Whichever route you choose, work closely with venue management and city officials as your crowd grows. Security and safety regulations become more intensive at high capacities – you’ll need to adhere to fire marshal limits for each room, plan for crowd control in common areas, and possibly hire professional security firms or off-duty police for traffic and safety. Large convention centers often require using union labour for tasks like booth setup or rigging, which adds cost and complexity. Additionally, major venues book out far in advance (sometimes years), so secure your future dates early. The logistics of load-in/load-out also scale up – moving 100 vendor booths and 5,000 attendees is one thing, but moving 500 booths and 100,000 attendees through loading docks, elevators, and escalators demands a detailed plan and experienced crew. The bottom line is space enables growth : give yourself the capacity, then scale into it with strong operations. Skimp on space and the fan experience will quickly suffer from overcrowding. Turning Superfans Into Growth Ambassadors — Rewarding loyal attendees for bringing friends creates a sustainable, community-driven marketing engine that scales organically. To illustrate, here’s a snapshot of how key metrics might scale when a convention grows from 2,000 to 100,000 attendees: Metric Small Fan Con (?2,000 attendees) Mega Fan Con (?100,000 attendees) Venue Size Hotel ballroom or campus hall (?2,000 m²) Single location City convention center (?50,000+ m²) plus overflow venues Multiple locations Programming Tracks 2–3 tracks (anime screenings, panels, etc.) 15+ tracks spanning genres (panels, screenings, gaming, workshops, etc.) Featured Guests 3–5 guests (local creators, niche celebs) 50+ guests (A-list actors, creators, industry panels across fandoms) Exhibitors & Artists ~30 vendor/artist tables (local shops, fan art) 300+ exhibitors (major brands, merch companies, artists alley, fan clubs) Volunteers & Staff ~30 volunteers, all part-time Core team of 5 organisers 800–1,000+ volunteers across departments Professional staff leads for ops, security, AV, etc. Budget (Operating Costs) Approx. $50,000 (venue, basic A/V, guests, marketing) $5–10 million+ (large venue rental, pro A/V & staging, star guests, extensive marketing) Hotel Room Blocks None or informal (attendees book on their own) Official room blocks at 5–10 hotels; travel partnerships for attendees (discounted rates, shuttles) Badge Types General admission only; simple paper badges Tiered badges (single-day, weekend, VIP, premium experiences); RFID or QR-coded badges for scanning (Metrics above are illustrative; actual figures vary by event.) As shown, a 100k-attendee convention operates on a different magnitude entirely. Yet, if managed well, it can still feel like a collection of intimate experiences rather than a faceless crowd. The key is scaling each aspect – venue, programming, vendors, staff, and amenities – in harmony so that no one element lags behind the others. Mastering Crowd Management and Flow With great crowds comes great responsibility – namely, preventing those crowds from turning into a logistical nightmare. Crowd management is one of the trickiest challenges as conventions grow, often distinguishing smooth events from disorganized ones. The fundamentals (clear signage, sensible layout, and plenty of staff) become absolutely critical at scale. Start by analyzing your traffic flow: how will 50,000 people circulate between panel rooms, the exhibit hall, food areas, and restrooms? Techniques like one-way corridors or designated “up” and “down” staircases can prevent jams. Tape on the floor marking lanes or waiting areas (a tactic Anime Expo effectively uses to guide attendees ) can avoid free-for-all clusters. Work with your venue’s fire marshal to identify chokepoints and establish overflow spaces where crowds can spill into if needed. Queuing systems deserve special attention. Fans will happily line up for must-see panels or exclusives, but long waits can sour the experience if handled poorly. As your con grows, implement advanced queue management tactics to keep lines orderly and people informed. Many large cons deploy a ticket or wristband system for the most popular panel sessions – for example, distributing morning wristbands for later big panels so that only those with bands wait, while others are free to enjoy other content. Digital solutions are increasingly common too: some events use virtual queue apps where attendees can join a line via smartphone and get notified when it’s their turn, reducing physical waiting. According to veteran organizers, adopting such crowd management strategies can make the difference between a fan-friendly mega-event and a chaotic mess. Even simple steps like providing line entertainment, water stations, and up-to-the-minute information (“Panel room full – please enjoy our overflow live stream in Hall B”) go a long way to maintain goodwill. Don’t forget external crowd logistics as well. Large conventions can impact the whole surrounding area – think traffic jams and mile-long badge pickup lines outside the venue. Coordinate with local authorities on traffic flow and public transport; many huge cons arrange shuttle buses from key parking lots or transit hubs to discourage everyone driving separately. Staggered check-in times or mailing out badges in advance can prevent a crush on Day 1. Line management outside the doors matters too – use railings or switchbacks for any queue that might snake around the block, and have staff or volunteers on crowd duty even in outdoor lines (with radios to call in extra support or medical help if needed). The best conventions create a detailed crowd control plan each year, often led by someone with safety or large-event experience. As one might expect, plans can be tested by reality – a sudden rainstorm, an unexpected celebrity entourage causing crowding, etc. That’s why having contingency protocols (like temporarily halting entry, opening an extra hall early, or using staff to disperse a tight crowd) is vital. By anticipating bottlenecks and actively managing crowds, you ensure that even tens of thousands of fans can navigate your event without feeling lost in an overwhelming sea of people. Mastering High-Volume Crowd Management Tactics — Strategic floor layouts and real-time communication keep tens of thousands of fans moving safely and efficiently through the venue. Building a Scalable Crew and Operations Team From Fan Volunteers to a Structured Workforce Most fan conventions begin as labours of love – a handful of enthusiasts wearing multiple hats and assisted by volunteer friends or club members. This familial approach can start an event off with great community spirit. However, as attendance grows into the thousands, you’ll need to expand and formalize your workforce to maintain quality and safety. The transition from a 20-person volunteer crew to a 500-person multi-tiered team is huge, and it’s one that veteran con organizers emphasize must be handled deliberately. Begin by defining a clear organization structure for your convention team. At small scale, everyone might report to one director; at large scale, you’ll require departments and team leads. Common units for big cons include Operations, Programming, Guest Relations, Vendor/Exhibit Hall, Registration, Security, Cosplay Ops, Hospitality (green room & guest transport), and Marketing/Press. Create lead roles for each area – ideally filled by people with prior experience – and delineate their responsibilities. For example, when you hit 10,000+ attendees, you may need a dedicated Volunteer Coordinator to recruit, train and manage all volunteers (whereas at 2,000 attendees, volunteers were informal and self-managed). By 50,000 attendees, expect to have several paid staff or contractors in key positions like security chief, PR manager, and technical director. Don’t be afraid to bring in experts from the festival or trade show world for critical operations roles; their knowledge can save you from learning by trial-and-error when the stakes are high. Recruiting and retaining a large volunteer force is an ongoing challenge. Free badges and a T-shirt might be enough incentive for a weekend volunteer shift at a small con, but larger events demand more time and skills from their crew. To build a reliable team, focus on culture and perks : foster camaraderie with team meetups or an opening-night volunteer party, offer behind-the-scenes experiences or exclusive swag, and publicly recognize outstanding helpers. Many conventions have a tiered system where volunteers who put in more hours get additional rewards (meals, travel stipends, exclusive photo ops with guests, etc.). It’s also crucial to provide proper training as your volunteer pool grows. Have written guides or online training modules for each role – whether it’s how to check badges at doors, how to manage line caps, or conflict resolution 101. Seasoned con runners know that investing in volunteer training dramatically reduces on-site fires to put out. Simple steps like briefing everyone on the code of conduct, radio protocols, and emergency procedures can prevent incidents and empower volunteers to handle issues before they escalate. Building A Structured Convention Workforce — Transitioning from informal volunteers to departmentalized teams provides the professional oversight needed to manage mega-event complexities. As you scale, you might worry about losing the “by fans, for fans” heart of your event by bringing in professional staff or more formal rules. In practice, structure actually helps volunteers shine by giving them the support and clarity to do their jobs well. When everyone knows their role and has the resources they need, the team can deliver that same friendly fan experience even to tens of thousands of attendees. A great example is Anime Expo in Los Angeles – it grew to over 100,000 attendees while still relying on a huge volunteer squad called “Arcade Staffers”. They succeeded by clearly delineating tasks and appointing veteran volunteers as area supervisors each year, ensuring crowds didn’t overwhelm the volunteer staff . The result was an event where volunteers felt ownership and pride, attendees got help and answers when they needed, and the once small con scaled up without losing its fan-driven soul. Training, Communication, and Leadership at Scale Effective internal communication becomes the make-or-break factor for operations as your convention grows. With a small team in one room, it’s easy to stay on the same page. But if you have 500 staff and volunteers spread across a convention center and nearby hotels, chaos can ensue unless you have robust communication channels. Equip your team leads with radios (and train them in concise radio etiquette to keep channels clear). Establish a chain of command for decision-making – for instance, the registration team leader can solve most badge issues, but anything involving refunds or VIP complaints escalates to the Operations Director. This hierarchy ensures front-line crew can act decisively without always “finding the boss”, which is critical when thousands of attendees need timely service. Regular team check-ins and briefings are also vital. Large conventions often start each day with a quick all-hands meeting or a distributed briefing (department heads meet with their teams) to update everyone on any changes, big schedule items, or issues from the previous day. Encourage a culture where staff feel comfortable reporting problems and ideas up the chain. As the event unfolds, have a “situation room” or central operations center where key staff monitor communications and coordinate responses. For example, if a big panel is reaching capacity, security can alert ops, who then inform the programming team to start an overflow stream and send a push notification to attendees. This kind of cross-team coordination is only possible if you’ve set up the infrastructure – shared chat groups, radio nets, a command post – and practiced it. Some cons run tabletop simulations or walkthroughs pre-event to train leadership in handling various scenarios (from medical emergencies to a surprise guest appearance that draws crowds). RFID Cashless Event Technology Get Started Free Another aspect to plan for is specialised training as your team grows. Consider bringing in professionals to train volunteers on things like crowd management, disability awareness, or conflict de-escalation. When your con was small, you might never have encountered a serious medical situation or a harassment complaint; at scale, these will happen, and your crew must be ready to respond appropriately and empathetically. Large events typically coordinate with local EMTs and have ambulances on standby, as well as establish a clear protocol for staff to report any safety or harassment issues (many cons now have a dedicated safety team or “Attendee Services” team to handle these incidents discreetly). By investing in training and clearly communicating roles and procedures, you build a trustworthy operation that can handle the pressures of a massive crowd. Finally, don’t overlook team morale . Long hours and high stress are common in convention operations, especially for multi-day events. As you grow, budget for basic crew welfare: provide a break room with snacks and water, schedule shifts so no one works a 12-hour stretch without relief, and consider bringing in a few floater volunteers who can step in so others get breaks to eat and rest. Burnt-out staff or volunteers can lead to mistakes that ripple through the attendee experience. A well-treated team, on the other hand, will go the extra mile to keep the convention magic alive for everyone. The mark of a smoothly scaled event is when even behind the scenes, there’s an organized, positive team culture powering the whole show. Leveraging Technology and Ticketing as You Scale Upgrading Ticketing and Registration Systems In the early days, your ticketing might have been as simple as an online form, PayPal account, or on-site cash sales with paper badges. To handle tens of thousands of attendees, robust ticketing technology is non-negotiable. First, you’ll want a platform that can easily support tiered badge types (weekend vs. single-day, VIP passes, exhibitor badges, press passes, etc.) and high-volume on-sales without crashing. Nothing frustrates fans more than a Ticketmaster-style meltdown during badge release. Modern solutions – such as an all-in-one event ticketing platform with built-in marketing and analytics – are built to queue transaction loads and prevent overselling, so invest in a reliable system that can scale with your attendance. Powering Seamless On-Site Transactions — Cashless payment systems speed up vendor lines and enhance financial security for both attendees and exhibitors. As your convention grows, consider adding features like RFID badges or QR codes for quick scanning. RFID-enabled badges (or wristbands) allow for much faster entry throughput, since attendees can just tap sensors at doors instead of having barcodes manually scanned. They also open up possibilities like cashless payments or access control for specific areas (e.g. VIP lounge or 18+ panels). For example, New York Comic Con switched to RFID badges as it grew past 100k attendees to combat counterfeit passes and speed up entry. If RFID feels too advanced, at least ensure your badge printing and scanning setup is industrial-grade – multiple printers, backup scanners, and a network that can handle on-site database lookups for thousands of records. The check-in process is every attendee’s first impression each day; by 2026, fans expect a swift, tech-assisted entry, not an hour waiting in line because of a slow ID check. Another essential tech upgrade is a robust online registration portal that handles all the new complexities of a big event. This might include badge mailing , where tickets purchased in advance are mailed as badges or QR codes to reduce on-site queues. It can also include integrated add-on sales (for booking special events, merchandise, or photo-ops in advance) so that these transactions are spread out and organized. A system with group and team ticketing is helpful if you’re expanding into esports or competitions – for instance, esports tournament ticketing features for team sign-ups and spectator passes ensure those events run smoothly alongside the main convention. As your event scales, it often gains multiple “sub-events” (tournaments, workshops, VIP experiences) that need their own capacity management within the wider con – a capable ticketing platform can automate that rather than relying on manual spreadsheets. Behind the scenes, large conventions benefit from the data and analytics modern ticketing provides. When you’re selling 50,000 badges, you can glean insights like where attendees are traveling from, which promotions sold the most tickets, and what the peak entry times are each day. Real-time dashboards allow you to adjust operations on the fly – for example, if you see a surge of Saturday single-day ticket scans between 9–10am, you might deploy more staff to the main entrance during that window . Data also guides growth decisions: by tracking attendance patterns, you can identify if adding a day (say a Thursday preview night) might better spread crowds, or if certain content is under-capacity and could be swapped out next year. The bottom line is that technology becomes your ally in scaling. By choosing the right ticketing and registration tools, you reduce friction for attendees and gain control over the complex moving parts of a massive convention. Streamlining Entry With RFID Technology — Advanced badge systems reduce morning entry queues and provide valuable data to help you adjust operations on the fly. Tech-Forward Solutions for Fan Engagement and Safety Beyond ticketing, a host of other technologies can help a big convention run smoothly. Mobile apps have become commonplace for fan events – by 2026, attendees expect a dedicated event app or mobile schedule at minimum. An official convention app lets fans personalize their schedule, get panel reminders, and receive push notifications for important updates (“Autograph session with Guest X starts in 10 minutes at Hall A”). This not only enhances the attendee experience but also aids crowd management – you can instantly alert everyone to changes or issues. For example, if a major guest’s panel is rescheduled, an app notification can prevent a roomful of angry fans. Some apps even show real-time room capacities or queue status, so attendees can decide on the fly which activities to pursue. Investing in a white-label event app or partnering with a service like Grenadine or Guidebook is well worth it when your event spans multiple days and venues. Large conventions are also embracing RFID and cashless payment systems for on-site purchases. Concession lines and merchandise booths move much faster when attendees can tap their badge or a stored payment wristband instead of fumbling with cash or cards, a strategy that helps manage massive convention attendance numbers . This is especially valuable if your con has large concerts, after-parties, or festival-style outdoor areas as part of the experience – going cashless reduces theft risk and makes financial tracking easier. Just be sure to also offer an easy way for fans to load these cashless accounts and a fallback for those who aren’t tech-savvy (like a onetime top-up booth for RFID wristbands). Similarly, incorporating contactless entry gates or turnstiles at main entrances can handle huge volumes; many events still use staff scanning, but turnstiles with badge tap readers can greatly increase throughput if configured well. A guide comparing entry tech options suggests that for crowds above 50k, hybrid approaches (staff with handheld scanners at early rush then turnstiles for steady flow) can optimize speed and flexibility. Safety technology is another area to leverage. As crowds grow, so does the importance of things like facial recognition for badge name checks (some cons use this to catch banned individuals or known ticket scammers) and real-time people counting systems to monitor venue density. If your budget allows, deploying CCTV cameras in key areas and having a security control center helps in managing incidents – it’s what many large-scale event organizers do for rapid response. Even simpler, ensure your staff and volunteers all have a reliable communication tech: push-to-talk apps or radios with dedicated channels for different teams (security, medical, ops) will speed up responses. For example, if there’s a medical emergency in the expo hall, any staffer should be able to radio “Code Blue at Exhibit Aisle 5” and trigger the med team without delay. At high volumes, instant communication and data can literally save lives and prevent minor hiccups from snowballing. One more tech-enabled aspect to consider is the online experience of your convention. As you surpass tens of thousands of attendees, inevitably many fans who can’t attend in person will want to be involved. Streaming large panels or hosting virtual content (like digital meet-and-greets or an online artist alley) can expand your reach without adding physical crowding. Events such as Comic-Con and Gamescom have successfully run hybrid editions where keynotes are broadcast globally, generating additional revenue and fan goodwill. While the logistics of hybrid events are a topic of their own, be aware that scaling in-person doesn’t mean you must ignore the online audience – they can be part of your growth strategy too, especially in 2026 where virtual access is a norm. Just be cautious not to detract from the live attendees’ value; for example, you might stream only certain content or offer exclusive online perks that don’t take away from the on-site experience. Expanding Reach Through Hybrid Programming — Streaming marquee content allows you to satisfy global demand and manage venue capacity without turning fans away. Preserving the Fan Experience and Community Magic Maintaining the Close-Knit Community Feel Amid all the logistical and commercial considerations of scaling up, never forget the heart of any fan convention: the community. The magic that longtime attendees speak of often comes from small, personal moments – a friendly conversation in line, a chance meeting with a favorite artist at the hotel bar, an inside joke at closing ceremonies. When your event grows 50x its original size, it’s easy for attendees to feel like just another face in a huge crowd unless you actively work to maintain a sense of community . One strategy is to keep some fan-made and fan-run elements as you expand. For instance, fan panels and meetups can be a staple of large cons just as they are in small ones – you might set aside a few rooms for community-submitted sessions or niche fandom meetups even if the main stages are filled with celebrity spotlights. This gives die-hard community members a stake in the event and lets new attendees immediately plug into like-minded groups. Traditions and signature activities also help make a big con still feel unique and familiar. If your 2,000-person event had a quirky tradition (say, a charity pie-in-the-face event for the con chair, or a themed cosplay parade), carry it forward and scale it up. Dragon Con, for example, has kept its fan-hosted parade through downtown Atlanta as a marquee event even as the con grew huge – it’s an anchor of fan pride that makes the city part of the experience. Similarly, Anime Expo preserved things like its late-night maid café and cosplay masquerade contests as it expanded, ensuring core fan culture stayed front and center by building a dedicated volunteer team and maintaining unique fan-focused programming . These familiar touchpoints make veterans feel at home and newcomers sense the event’s personality beyond just big crowds and commerce. Turn Fans Into Your Marketing Team Ticket Fairy's built-in referral rewards system incentivizes attendees to share your event, delivering 15-25% sales boosts and 30x ROI vs paid ads. Referral Marketing for Events Get Started Free Communication with your fan community becomes more important, not less, as you scale. Large conventions like San Diego Comic-Con hold an open feedback forum (the “Comic-Con Talk Back” panel) at the end of each event, where attendees can voice complaints and suggestions directly to organizers. This kind of listening ear signals that fan input matters, even if the con is now a behemoth. You don’t have to wait for the event itself – use surveys, social media, and community forums year-round to gauge sentiment. When fans see their suggestions implemented (“you asked for more water stations and we added them” or “due to feedback, we’ll have a quiet room for those needing a break from crowds”), it builds loyalty and trust. The narrative should be “we’re growing this together” rather than a faceless corporate expansion. Transparency about challenges helps too; if you have to increase badge prices or enforce stricter rules as you grow, explain the reasons to your community. Fans might grumble, but they’ll appreciate being treated like stakeholders, not just customers. Finally, invest in the emotional and social experience of attendees, not just the spectacle. Big conventions can be exhausting and overwhelming – plan features that humanize the experience. For example, create dedicated rest areas or lounges where people can sit, recharge (devices and themselves), and meet fellow fans in a calmer setting. Offer interactive elements that spark joy at any scale, like community art walls where attendees can doodle, or scavenger hunts that encourage making new friends. Emphasize inclusivity and safety so fans know the expanded crowd doesn’t mean more tolerance for bad behavior. Initiatives like harassment reporting systems, cosplay repair stations , gender-neutral bathrooms, and quiet zones for neurodivergent or anxious attendees all contribute to a welcoming atmosphere. When fans see that even at 100,000 strong, the convention still cares about each person’s experience, the magic endures. In essence, never lose sight of why people come in the first place – to celebrate their passions with others. If every decision, from scaling a venue to booking a guest, is filtered through the lens of “will this delight our community?”, you’ll be well on your way to growing in size while staying true to your roots. Preserving Intimacy Within Massive Crowds — Dedicated quiet zones and inclusive amenities ensure that even the largest events feel welcoming and attentive to individual needs. Frequently Asked Questions What is a multi-venue strategy for fan conventions? A multi-venue strategy involves hosting a single convention across several nearby locations, such as convention centers and adjacent hotels, rather than one building. Events like New York Comic Con and Dragon Con use this approach to accommodate over 65,000 to 200,000 attendees without severe overcrowding. How do organizers manage crowds at large fan conventions? Organizers manage massive convention crowds by implementing virtual queue apps, designated one-way corridors, and floor tape to guide traffic flow. Distributing morning wristbands for popular afternoon panels and utilizing overflow live-stream rooms also prevents dangerous bottlenecks and keeps attendees informed in real-time. What is a safe annual growth rate for a fan convention? A safe and sustainable growth rate for fan conventions is typically 15 to 20 percent annually. This gradual pacing allows organizers to scale infrastructure, secure larger venues, and train additional volunteer staff without compromising safety or overwhelming the intimate fan experience. What are the benefits of using RFID badges at large events? RFID badges significantly speed up entry throughput by allowing attendees to tap sensors instead of waiting for manual barcode scans. This technology also combats counterfeit passes, enables cashless on-site payments for merchandise, and provides organizers with real-time data on peak entry times and crowd density. How can organizers increase fan convention attendance organically? Launching a fan referral program is the most effective way to organically grow convention attendance. By offering incentives like exclusive pins or ticket discounts for bringing friends, organizers can turn passionate attendees into a street team, often boosting overall ticket sales by 15 to 25 percent. How much do celebrity guests charge for convention appearances? Top-tier Hollywood actors and celebrity talent typically charge appearance fees ranging from $25,000 to over $250,000 per convention. Organizers must also budget for additional logistical expenses, including first-class travel, premium lodging, and daily per-diems, often requiring corporate sponsorships to underwrite these massive costs. How do mega conventions organize their volunteer staff? Massive conventions organize volunteers by establishing a structured hierarchy with dedicated departments like Operations, Guest Relations, and Security. Appointing experienced veteran volunteers as area supervisors and providing tiered rewards, such as travel stipends or exclusive photo ops, ensures a reliable and well-trained workforce. How can massive fan conventions maintain an intimate community feel? Large conventions preserve their close-knit vibe by hosting niche fan-run panels, maintaining signature traditions like cosplay parades, and creating dedicated quiet lounges. Actively listening to attendee feedback through post-event forums and implementing fan suggestions ensures the community feels valued despite the massive crowd size.

Projects change that. Add participants to a test , bringing in more synthetic users whenever you want a stronger signal, without starting a brand-new test. title: Inbox Zero Is the Wrong Goal
summary: Chasing an empty inbox optimizes the wrong metric. Here is what an intelligent inbox optimizes instead.
body_text: Why is inbox zero the wrong goal? Because an empty inbox measures activity, not outcomes. You can hit zero by archiving everything and still miss the three threads that actually mattered. The better target is making sure the email that moves your work forward gets handled, and the rest stays out of the way. Slashy optimizes for that by auto-labeling inbound mail and surfacing the threads that need you, instead of rewarding you for clearing a count. What should I optimize for instead of an empty inbox? Response on the threads that matter and nothing dropped on the ones you owe. Slashy ships follow-up reminders with ghost detection, so an outbound thread that goes quiet gets surfaced rather than forgotten. Open tracking shows who actually read your email. Those signals tell you whether you are keeping commitments, which is the real job, not whether the unread badge says zero. How does Slashy decide what needs my attention? It auto-labels inbound mail into Important, Calendar, Billing, Newsletter, Order, Other, and Work, then surfaces the high-priority threads first. The classification is behavior-trained, so it learns from what you open and reply to rather than running fixed rules. The in-house memory system keeps adjusting as your patterns shift, which is why prioritization gets more accurate over weeks instead of staying frozen at day one. Does an intelligent inbox just hide email from me? No. Nothing is deleted. Low-priority mail is sorted into labels like Newsletter and Other so it stays out of your primary view, and you can open any label whenever you want. The point is sequencing, not hiding: the threads that matter come first, and the rest waits in a place you can still reach. You decide what to act on; Slashy decides the order it reaches you. Will Slashy draft replies so I can clear important threads faster? Yes. Slashy drafts replies in your tone with one-click send, and acceptance climbs from around 30% on day 1 to over 80% by day 30 as the memory system learns your voice. So the threads that do need a response take a keystroke rather than a blank page. The goal is not to empty the inbox, it is to close the loops that count without the drafting friction.
